hints: Look closely at the central carbon in the diagram. Count the four different groups attached to it and notice which one looks like a simple side chain.
Remember the general structure of an amino acid: every amino acid has the same $NH_2$, $COOH$ and $H$, so only the fourth group, the R group, varies.
walkthrough:
**Recall what all amino acids share**

Every amino acid has the same basic backbone. There is a central carbon joined to an amino group ($NH_2$), a carboxyl group ($COOH$), and a hydrogen atom.

General structure:
$$central\ C - NH_2 + central\ C - COOH + central\ C - H$$

**Spot the variable R group in this diagram**

In your diagram the central C is joined to $NH_2$ on the left, $COOH$ ($C=O$ plus $OH$) on the right, and $H$ below. The fourth group on top is $CH_3$.

That $CH_3$ is the R group. In this example it makes the amino acid alanine.

**Decide what changes**

To make a different amino acid, the $NH_2$, $C=O$, $OH$ and $H$ stay the same. Only the R group is swapped for a different side chain. So the $CH_3$ is the group that is changed.

options.A: The OH is part of the carboxyl group ($COOH$) found in every amino acid, so it does not vary.
options.B: The C=O is also part of the carboxyl group ($COOH$) found in every amino acid, so it does not vary.
options.C: The $CH_3$ is the R side chain on the central carbon. Changing the R group produces the 20 different amino acids.
options.D: The $NH_2$ is the amino group found in every amino acid, so it does not vary.
